vignette:
A 74-year-old man with a history of metastatic prostate cancer and a known left upper lobe lung mass presented with four weeks of progressive vertigo, described as the sensation that “the floor was wobbling” and “the room was swaying,” leading to difficulty ambulating. A few days before admission, he developed severe bifrontal throbbing headaches with nausea and vomiting. Two days prior, he was evaluated at an outside emergency department, tested positive for adenovirus, and was discharged after supportive treatment without symptom relief.

His oncology history included stage III prostate adenocarcinoma treated with prostatectomy and radiation in 2013, followed by detection of bilateral lung nodules and sclerotic bone lesions in 2016, and a 2020 biopsy of a left upper lobe lesion confirming mismatch repair deficient, androgen receptor–positive metastatic prostate cancer treated with enzalutamide, then abiraterone acetate and prednisone, and palliative radiation.

On presentation, vital signs were: temperature 37°C, heart rate 90 beats/min, blood pressure 164/81 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 93% on room air. Neurologic examination revealed no focal motor or sensory deficits; intact coordination on dysdiadochokinesia, finger-to-nose, and heel-to-shin testing; an intact gait despite dizziness; and a positive right-sided Dix–Hallpike maneuver with horizontal nystagmus.

Noncontrast head CT showed a 3 cm left cerebellar hemispheric mass with surrounding vasogenic edema causing mild partial effacement of the fourth ventricle and left quadrigeminal cistern. The patient received dexamethasone. MRI of the brain demonstrated a cystic enhancing lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere with mass effect; no other intra-axial lesions were identified. Cerebral angiography revealed no abnormal hyperemia at the site of the lesion.

A hemangioblastoma was considered the leading diagnosis; other considerations included metastases and infarction.

A 21-year-old woman with autism spectrum disorder (on risperidone) and intellectual disability was brought to the hospital after a witnessed collapse. She had no prior history of syncope, cardiac arrest, or known cardiovascular disease, and her family denied any illicit drug or alcohol use. While at a noisy auto mechanic shop, she became pale and lost consciousness; bystander ECG showed ventricular fibrillation. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after two defibrillations. On arrival, her blood pressure was 93/70 mmHg, pulse 86 bpm, and oxygen saturation 100% (bag–valve–mask). An intravenous amiodarone infusion (1 mg/min) and oral amiodarone 400 mg were administered. On examination she was comatose (GCS 3), with agonal respirations; cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. In the intensive care unit, her differential diagnosis included channelopathies, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and metabolic abnormalities. Laboratory tests showed normal chemistry panel and electrolytes. Initial electrocardiogram revealed sinus rhythm with interpolated premature ventricular complexes and a QTc of 380 ms, without any evidence of infarction, pre-excitation, or Brugada pattern. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 45–50%, normal wall thickness, and no valvular abnormalities.

A 14-year-old girl presented with 2 months of progressive proximal muscle weakness. She initially noted difficulty combing her hair and rising from a chair; over weeks she became wheelchair-bound. She also reported morning stiffness of both small hand joints lasting about 30 minutes, dysphagia for solids and liquids, and poor appetite, without fever or weight loss.

Her medical history was notable for thyroiditis in 2015 that resolved without long-term therapy. Family history included a younger sister with Prader–Willi syndrome. She was up to date on vaccinations.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologic testing showed symmetric muscle strength of 4/5 in the upper limbs and 3/5 in the lower limbs, with brisk reflexes more pronounced on the left. She could not stand from the wheelchair unaided. In the left hand, she was unable to make a fist or tuck the fingers; there was tenderness at the fourth and fifth proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed leukopenia (WBC 2.96 × 10^3/µL), microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL), elevated C-reactive protein (18.8 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (109.2 mm/hr), and normal creatine kinase (39 U/L). Thyroid function tests showed suppressed TSH (0.017 µIU/mL), elevated free T4 (20.9 pmol/L), normal free T3 (4.53 pmol/L), and markedly elevated anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (3410 IU/mL). Antinuclear antibody titer was 27 (reference <20); rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, and ANCA were negative. Viral serologies, renal and liver tests, and other hormonal assays were normal.

Hyperkalemic paralysis was ruled out. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a multinodular goiter consistent with thyroiditis. MRI of the brain and lumbosacral spine was normal; cervical spine MRI showed a small C6–C7 disc herniation. Incidentally, the lumbosacral spine MRI revealed bilateral sacroiliitis. Dedicated MRI of the sacroiliac joints confirmed bilateral sacroiliitis; HLA-B27 was negative. MRI of the hips and pelvis showed bilateral thigh intramuscular edema with enhancement. Although myositis was suspected, electromyography and repeat creatine kinase were normal.

vignette:
A 48-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension presented with bilateral breast lumps of one-week duration. She had no family history of breast or ovarian cancer and had previously regular menstrual cycles. On examination, the left breast had a 4 × 4 cm hard lump in the lower inner quadrant fixed to the chest wall; the right breast had a firm, mobile 1 × 1 cm lump in the lower outer quadrant. MRI showed a 3.8 × 3.5 cm irregular spiculated mass in the left breast suspicious for malignancy and a 2.3 × 1.5 cm well-defined lesion in the right breast with a type 1 contrast enhancement pattern (< 6% probability of malignancy) and bilateral axillary lymphadenopathy. Ultrasound and bone scan were negative for metastases. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the left breast lump revealed poorly cohesive clusters of ductal cells with pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, and prominent nucleoli; myoepithelial cells and bare nuclei were absent. FNAC of the left axillary lymph node showed similar malignant cells. FNAC of the right breast lump showed three-dimensional clusters of hyperchromatic cells with prominent nucleoli and scattered pleomorphic cells with mitotic figures admixed with benign ductal cells and myoepithelial cells; a few bare nuclei were seen. Cytologic diagnosis was duct cell carcinoma of both breasts with left axillary lymph node metastasis. A core-needle biopsy of the left breast confirmed infiltrative duct cell carcinoma that was estrogen- and progesterone-receptor positive. On the basis of the physical examination results, the right breast lump was suspected to be a fibroadenoma. Hence, lumpectomy was performed.

vignette:
A 54-year-old African American woman with poorly controlled hypertension, a 15 pack-year smoking history, and alpha-thalassemia anemia presented after 3 weeks of progressive blurred vision, fatigue, headache, and orthopnea. She was referred for hypertensive retinopathy evaluation, where her blood pressure measured 220/130 mmHg and she had cotton-wool spots on funduscopic exam. In the emergency department, her systolic pressure reached 230 mmHg. On examination, jugular venous pressure was 14 cm above the sternal angle; heart sounds were distant without pulsus paradoxus; lungs were clear; and there was no peripheral edema. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL (baseline 10 g/dL), creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, C-reactive protein 11 mg/L, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate 110 mm/hr. Chest radiography demonstrated a markedly enlarged cardiac silhouette with mild pulmonary congestion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large circumferential pericardial effusion (2.24 cm) with early right ventricular diastolic collapse, respirophasic mitral inflow variation, and a dilated inferior vena cava. Contrast-enhanced CT angiography of the chest and cardiac MRI showed no pericardial or pleural thickening, masses, or aortic dissection. She underwent pericardiocentesis yielding 1160 mL of straw-colored fluid. A rheumatologic workup revealed an antinuclear antibody titer of 1:640, positive anti-Smith antibodies, and low complement levels (C3, C4). High-dose intravenous steroids were administered, and a repeat echocardiogram two days later showed reduction of the effusion. Pericardial fluid cytology showed few reactive mesothelial cells and a predominantly lymphocytic infiltrate; bacterial, viral, and fungal studies were negative. Immunohistochemical staining of the fluid was positive for calretinin and weakly positive for CK5/6 and MOC31.

vignette:
A 74-year-old Spanish-speaking man visiting the United States from Honduras presented with a 2-month history of postprandial abdominal pain, nausea, night sweats, early satiety, and a 10-kg weight loss. One week earlier, an abdominal and pelvic CT scan had shown distal ileitis, and he had received a course of antibiotics without improvement. On re-presentation, he reported worsening symptoms and difficulty tolerating oral intake. He denied hematochezia, diarrhea, or fevers. His medical history was notable for prior appendectomy and recently treated helminth infection.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. There was no abdominal tenderness or palpable masses, and no evidence of perianal disease. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 42 mm/hr, a C-reactive protein level of 35 mg/L, and a fecal calprotectin of 94 μg/mg. Stool studies were negative for enteric pathogens. Repeat CT imaging demonstrated persistent distal ileitis.

Ileocolonoscopy revealed a normal terminal ileum, but a nontraversable distal ileal stricture, cecal ulcers, and patchy loss of vascularity throughout the colon. Segmental biopsies of the ileum and colon were obtained. QuantiFERON-TB Gold was positive. Hepatitis B serologies showed a reactive core total antibody, a reactive e antigen, negative surface antigen, and undetectable HBV DNA. He was started on isoniazid for latent tuberculosis.

vignette:
A 33-year-old Hispanic man with no known past medical history presented with a 1½-week history of headache and blurred vision. MRI of the brain demonstrated a 2.7-cm ring-enhancing lesion in the right temporal lobe with mass effect. He underwent craniotomy with biopsy and resection. Postoperatively, he was found to have HIV infection with a CD4 count <20 cells/µL and an HIV viral load of 191 000 copies/mL. Serum toxoplasma IgG was elevated, and CSF studies showed 48 cells/µL (97% lymphocytes) with positive toxoplasma IgG and DNA-PCR for Toxoplasma gondii (286 copies/mL). Other CSF studies, including fungal cultures, cryptococcal antigen, and AFB smear/culture, were negative. Histopathologic examination of the brain tissue revealed bradyzoites and tachyzoites. He was treated with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole and started on antiretroviral therapy; empiric antibiotics for bacterial abscess were discontinued.

Two weeks after discharge, he returned with fever to 39.6 °C, generalized weakness, and a 1-day history of productive cough. Chest radiograph showed a new left upper lobe opacification with diffuse reticulonodular interstitial prominence. CT scan of the chest confirmed extensive reticulonodular interstitial infiltrates with focal consolidation in the left upper lobe. He was started on vancomycin, piperacillin/tazobactam, and fluconazole and placed on airborne precautions. His respiratory status worsened, and intubation was planned pending further diagnostic evaluation.

After extubation, he developed profound hypotension and pulmonary oedema. Transthoracic echocardiography showed severely impaired left ventricular (LV) systolic function. Coronary angiography revealed no evidence of relevant coronary artery disease, and toxicological screening was negative. His medical history included chronic polyarthritis and treated arterial hypertension.

On transfer, he was invasively ventilated (PaO2/FiO2 30 mmHg), receiving norepinephrine at 2.5 µg/kg/min. Blood pressure was 75/49 mmHg, heart rate 180 b.p.m., with bilateral rales and basal dullness on chest percussion. He experienced pulseless electrical activity requiring 5 minutes of resuscitation. Bedside echocardiography demonstrated akinesia of all basal and mid LV segments with preserved apical contraction (left ventricular ejection fraction, 15%); right ventricular function was preserved (TAPSE 17 mm). On the basis of these findings, reverse takotsubo cardiomyopathy was suspected. A percutaneous LV assist device (Impella CP®) was implanted immediately. Endomyocardial biopsy revealed moderate chronically active myocarditis with diffuse interstitial remodelling, and PCR testing showed no evidence of acute or persistent myocardial infection.

response.rationale: D7 (Angiomyolipoma) is the only diagnosis that fully explains the triad of fat attenuation, an intratumoral vascular pedicle, and a fatty tumor thrombus in the renal vein. D4 (Renal cell carcinoma with tumor thrombus) is close but does not account for fat attenuation; RCC rarely contains macroscopic fat and would produce a non-fatty tumor thrombus. Other RCC subtypes (D5, D6, D9) and generic RCC (D8) align even less with the fat component. Metastasis (D3) is improbable given fat attenuation and the absence of other lesions; the vascular pedicle argues for a renal primary. Liposarcoma (D10) could contain fat and thrombus but would not exhibit the distinct renal parenchymal vascular pedicle. Renal Vein Thrombosis (D1) lacks the mass and fat features. Thus D7 is the unequivocal best fit.

A 2-month-old full-term female with known complex congenital heart disease (single ventricle defect, double-outlet right ventricle with D-transposition of the great arteries, and an ostium secundum atrial septal defect with left superior vena cava) was admitted for evaluation of occasional cyanosis. The team planned a pulmonary artery banding, but during the procedure the patient became hemodynamically unstable and suffered a cardiorespiratory arrest requiring cardiac massage, so the operation was aborted. To gather hemodynamic data, cardiac catheterization was performed via the left femoral artery, with the catheter tip in the single ventricle, using serial doses of nonionic iodinated contrast (Iopromide) totaling 3 mL/kg over 30 minutes. vignette:
A 74-year-old Caucasian woman with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (diagnosed in 2006, complex karyotype with TP53 mutation and trisomy 12) was receiving zanubrutinib and subcutaneous immunoglobulin replacement for hypogammaglobulinemia. In May 2022 she was hospitalized for pulmonary sepsis, treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics and caspofungin, with resolution. One month later, she developed grade 4 neutropenia (<500/μL) for over 15 days and a febrile peak. Starting 15 June, tender, warm, erythematous nodular skin lesions appeared on the lower limbs and then the upper limbs; the lesions progressed to central ulceration with a necrotic core. 

On 25 June, zanubrutinib was discontinued and oral itraconazole was begun after a 5 mm punch biopsy of a left-thigh lesion. Histopathological examination (HE, Giemsa, GMS, PAS, and Gram stains) showed severe diffuse lympho-monocytic inflammation with minimal necrosis, angioinvasive microbial structures, thrombosed small vessels, and sparse hyphal mats with sporangial-type cells. Within vessels, thin-walled (5–15 μm), pauciseptate hyphae with minimal branching were seen, along with numerous thick-walled ovoid sporangia (5–20 μm) that stained strongly with PAS, GMS, and Giemsa. Only a presumptive diagnosis of deep cutaneous fungal infection was made at this time.

vignette:
A 45-year-old woman was admitted to an acute psychiatric hospital with depressed mood, suicidal ideation, and auditory hallucinations. She had been discharged five days earlier from another facility and had 18 emergency department visits in the prior year. Her psychiatric history included benzodiazepine use disorder, opiate use disorder, borderline personality disorder, and major depressive disorder. Home medications were clonazepam, clonidine, buprenorphine–naloxone, fluoxetine, gabapentin, and trazodone. She was unemployed, homeless, and without family support.

During the admission, she exhibited:
- Catatonia-like signs: flat affect with psychomotor retardation and fluctuating mutism; complete lack of social contact; twitching, eye grimacing, and shoulder shrugging; posturing and immobility; diaphoresis.
- Psychotic signs: mouthing words and seemingly responding to internal stimuli; thought blocking; reported auditory hallucinations.
- Seizure-like behavior: episodes of head jerking with eye fluttering without tongue biting; remained conversant; benign neurologic examination.

Clues suggesting volitional behavior included selective acceptance of benzodiazepines and gabapentin while refusing other medications, eating all meals despite “stupor,” abruptly lapsing into and out of catatonia-like and psychotic behaviors depending on the topic of conversation, purposeful movements to obtain lorazepam after seizures, and evidence of self‐induced urinary incontinence during one episode.

A regional catatonia specialist evaluated her and noted that she was unlikely to have catatonia. Repeated lorazepam challenge tests had limited effect on her behaviors and appeared to reinforce them.

vignette:
A male newborn was referred at 1 day of age for cyanosis; oxygen saturation (SaO2) was 80% in room air. Laboratory findings showed a hematocrit of 47.8% and a platelet count of 103 000/mm3; other values were normal and there were no signs of infection. Echocardiography revealed pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect and a patent ductus arteriosus. A prostaglandin infusion was started, raising SaO2 to 90–95%. On day 11, he underwent a systemic‐to‐pulmonary shunt operation with graft placement and PDA division. Preoperative values on day 10 were hematocrit 38.9%, platelet count 173 000/mm3, and SaO2 95% on prostaglandin. Postoperatively, hematocrit was 52.1% and platelet count was 58 000/mm3; platelet count then increased without transfusion. By postoperative day 6, he was extubated with SaO2 80–85%, hematocrit 41.1%, and platelet count 123 000/mm3. He was discharged on postoperative day 13 with SaO2 85–87%, hematocrit 33.4%, and platelet count 225 000/mm3.

At 10 months of age, he was admitted for a Rastelli operation. His SaO2 was 80%; hematocrit was 49.1% and platelet count was 68 000/mm3. He had no bleeding history or medications. Prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, and INR were normal; peripheral smear was unremarkable. Antiplatelet antibodies and platelet‐associated immunoglobulins were negative; antinuclear and anti–double‐stranded DNA antibodies were normal. Platelet aggregation time was 127 s (reference, 61–110 s). Viral and bacterial studies were insignificant. The pediatrician made a provisional diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia and administered intravenous immunoglobulins (2 g/kg) the day before surgery. On the day of operation, hematocrit was 42.6% and platelet count was 77 000/mm3.

vignette:
A man in his 50s with a 12-year history of recurrent follicular lymphoma presented with a subacute, multifocal, pruritic, painful eruption that began on the abdomen and then involved the scalp, groin, and extremities. He denied fevers, chills, weight loss, or other systemic symptoms. His medications included oxycodone, duvelisib (a PI3K inhibitor), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, all started 14 months earlier for lymphoma management. On examination, there were well-demarcated erythematous plaques on the abdomen, axillae, and inguinal folds; scattered erythematous scaly papules and plaques on the scalp, extremities, and hands; and confluent erythematous hyperkeratotic plaques with plate-like scales on the plantar feet. Two skin biopsies (abdomen and left foot) showed parakeratosis with collections of neutrophils, hypogranulosis, regular epidermal hyperplasia with elongated rete ridges, thin suprapapillary plates, dilated papillary dermal vessels, and dermal eosinophils, findings consistent with a psoriasiform drug reaction.

vignette:
A 70-year-old Japanese man presented with dysphagia and was diagnosed with T3N0M0 esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. His medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 6.6%), percutaneous coronary intervention, and radiotherapy for laryngeal cancer. He underwent two courses of 5-fluorouracil/docetaxel/cisplatin and then thoracoscopic esophagectomy with retrosternal gastric tube reconstruction and cervical esophagogastrostomy.

On postoperative day 4, cervical wound erythema with pus and saliva discharge appeared; drainage and intravenous tazobactam/piperacillin were initiated. Despite nutritional support and improved albumin levels, a refractory anastomotic fistula persisted, and Enterobacter cloacae was cultured from the wound. On day 60, salvage reconstruction with a free jejunal autograft and pectoralis major muscle flap coverage was performed.

Fifteen days after reconstruction, he developed worsening low back pain and fever (38.2 °C). Examination revealed lumbar spinal tenderness and bilateral leg weakness without sensory loss. Laboratory tests showed a white blood cell count of 9200/µL and C-reactive protein of 9.86 mg/dL. Chest radiography and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable. Blood cultures grew Enterobacter cloacae. MRI of the lumbar spine demonstrated decreased T1 signal and increased T2 and STIR signal at L4–L5.

response.rationale: The target sign on MRI is a hallmark of schwannoma, a benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor. The median nerve compression symptoms and radial wrist location are consistent with a schwannoma arising from the median nerve. Other candidates such as ganglion cyst or giant cell tumor of tendon sheath do not typically exhibit a biphasic target enhancement pattern.

rejected.why: Targetoid hemosiderotic hemangioma is a vascular lesion that does not typically cause median nerve compression or present with a target sign on contrast-enhanced MRI in this location.
Nodular tenosynovitis may cause a wrist mass but lacks the characteristic biphasic target enhancement and is not specifically associated with median nerve compression.
Ganglion cysts are cystic and do not show solid biphasic contrast enhancement; they are usually anechoic on MRI and do not have a target sign.
Giant cell tumor of tendon sheath is a solid wrist mass but typically shows low signal on T2 and does not have a target sign; it is less likely to cause isolated median nerve compression.
Synovial sarcoma is malignant and more aggressive, often with heterogeneous enhancement and not a classic target sign; the 1-year gradual course and well-defined encapsulation favor a benign process.
Glomus tumors are typically subungual, very painful, and not located on the radial wrist; they do not present with a target sign.
Lipomas are fat-containing and do not enhance with contrast in a biphasic pattern; they are not associated with median nerve compression.

A 61-year-old woman with type II diabetes presented with several days of urinary retention and inability to ambulate in the setting of a 1-year history of progressive lower-extremity weakness and a 100-lb unintentional weight loss. Her weakness began in the proximal left leg, gradually involved the right leg and both hands, and was accompanied by worsening numbness and tingling in her feet; she became wheelchair-dependent within 6 months. Sensation to light touch was reduced in the feet, with slight impairment of vibration and proprioception. Reflexes were 2+ in the upper extremities and absent at the knees and ankles; plantar responses were flexor. Bladder catheterization yielded 1.8 L of retained urine. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count; sodium 117 mmol/L; chloride 87 mmol/L; blood urea nitrogen 0.89 mg/dL; creatinine 25 mg/dL. Urine was negative for protein or bacteria. CSF analysis revealed protein 175 mg/dL, glucose 105 mg/dL, 1 WBC, 0 RBC; CSF cytology was negative for malignancy. Lyme serology, autoimmune panel, and a comprehensive paraneoplastic antibody panel were negative. Hemoglobin A1c was 6.5 g/dL. On hospital day 4, electromyography and nerve conduction studies demonstrated decreased amplitudes in motor and sensory nerves, slowed conduction velocities, prolonged distal latencies, and absent sensory responses, suggesting a chronic length-dependent sensorimotor demyelinating polyneuropathy with superimposed chronic lumbosacral plexopathy. MRI of the pelvis showed bilateral femoral nerve enlargement without enhancement.

vignette:
A 67-year-old man with hypertension, dyslipidaemia, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, active smoking (35 pack-years), a family history of ischaemic heart disease, and prior percutaneous coronary interventions (2008, 2017, 2022) for non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction presented with Canadian Cardiovascular Society Class III angina. A recent exercise stress test induced angina at 50 W without ECG changes. On admission, he appeared anxious; the physical examination was unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG showed normal sinus rhythm, Q waves in lead III, and biphasic T waves in leads III and aVF. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 65% without regional wall-motion abnormalities. Coronary angiography demonstrated patent stents in the circumflex artery, non-significant disease in the left anterior descending artery, and significant ostial right coronary artery stenosis with in-stent restenosis in the mid-segment, which was treated with three drug-eluting stents. After transfer to the intensive care unit, he complained of worsening chest pain; ECG showed ST-segment elevation in leads V1–V3, and echocardiography remained normal. A second angiogram showed patent stents but subocclusion of the right coronary postero-lateral branch, successfully treated with balloon angioplasty, relieving his pain. Shortly thereafter, he developed recurrent sustained polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation requiring seven external shocks and 15 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Post-resuscitation ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm with persistent precordial ST-segment elevation and new QTc prolongation to 500 ms. Repeat echocardiography revealed akinesia of all apical segments, later extending to mid-segments, hyperkinesia of the basal segments, and severely reduced LVEF of 35%, leading to suspicion of takotsubo syndrome.

A 34‐year‐old woman presented with pain and slight mobility of the mandibular right second premolar and first molar. Her medical history was unremarkable. vignette:
A 36-year-old woman with a 17-year history of migraine headaches was referred for management of a right-sided migraine characterized by a visual aura of gray-white spots followed by pain behind the right eye radiating to the right frontal, temporal, and suboccipital regions. She typically had 3 to 4 severe migraines per month lasting 3 to 7 days, with relief only from sumatriptan after trials of acetaminophen, ibuprofen, rizatriptan, methylprednisolone, prednisone, and dexamethasone failed. In January 2023, she developed a right orbital and medial cheek headache radiating to the right lateral jaw, ear, and down the right suboccipital region. Treatment with ketorolac, rizatriptan, and a 7-day dexamethasone taper failed to resolve her symptoms. She then received naratriptan, prochlorperazine, acetaminophen, ibuprofen, and diphenhydramine without improvement. Brain magnetic resonance imaging was unremarkable. Given refractory symptoms, she underwent an ultrasound-guided right sphenopalatine ganglion block with 4 mL of bupivacaine 0.25% and 1 mL of dexamethasone 4 mg/mL. This treatment also failed to resolve her symptoms.

vignette:
An 8-year-old, previously healthy, fully immunized girl presented with 5 days of intermittent fever followed by abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. She had been at home due to the COVID-19 pandemic; her parents had mild upper respiratory symptoms for 1 week. Outpatient oral antibiotics and IV fluids did not improve her symptoms. She was admitted to surgery with suspected appendicitis; abdominal ultrasonography was normal. Persistent fever, abdominal pain, and the emergence of a rash and conjunctivitis prompted transfer to the pediatric COVID-19 ward. 

On examination, temperature was 38.6 °C. She had bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, erythematous throat, palmar erythema, a strawberry tongue, and an erythema multiforme–type rash; there was no hypotension, lymphadenopathy, or respiratory distress. Cardiac examination revealed a grade II/VI murmur at the left sternal border; lung sounds were normal.

Laboratory tests showed ESR 67 mm/h, CRP 166 mg/L, platelet count 192×10^9/L, hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, and WBC 10.3×10^9/L with 82% neutrophils. Liver and renal function tests were normal. Urinalysis and urine culture were negative. A high-resolution chest CT scan was not indicative of COVID-19. Reverse transcription PCR for SARS-CoV-2 and blood cultures were negative.

vignette:
A 25-year-old Hispanic woman of African descent, previously healthy and a non-smoker, presented with a 1-month history of dyspnea on exertion, intermittent dry cough, hyporexia, and unquantified intermittent fever. She delayed care until an acute worsening of dyspnea led to emergency department evaluation, where she developed acute respiratory failure and pulseless electrical activity arrest. After orotracheal intubation and stabilization, she was transferred to our institution.

On arrival, she was sedated on mechanical ventilation. Vital signs were notable for blood pressure 200/140 mmHg, heart rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 16 bpm, temperature 36 °C, and oxygen saturation 78% on ventilatory support. Physical examination revealed anisocoria (right pupil 5 mm, left 3 mm), jugular venous distension, sinus tachycardia, and bilateral coarse rales; no skin lesions or peripheral edema were present.

Chest radiography showed a homogeneous right paratracheal mediastinal mass compressing and displacing the trachea to the left, with adjacent right upper-lobe infiltrates. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest and neck demonstrated an 11 × 8.6 × 9.5 cm lobulated solid mass arising from the right thoracic operculum/pleura, with a nodular pleural component, mass effect on the right hilum, supra-aortic vessels, and superior vena cava, pneumomediastinum, left pneumothorax, and lytic destruction with cortical fracture of the T1 and T2 vertebrae. Centrilobular opacities in the left upper lobe suggested aspiration pneumonitis.

Laboratory tests showed WBC 13.47 × 10^3/µL (85% neutrophils), hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL, platelets 303 × 10^3/µL, INR 1.39, lactic acid 2.83 mmol/L, C-reactive protein 4.20 mg/dL, LDH 592 U/L, calcium 6.58 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.73 mg/dL; arterial blood gas revealed pH 7.30, PCO2 44.5 mmHg, PO2 122 mmHg, HCO3 22.3 mmol/L, BE –3.7 mmol/L, and SO2 98%. She received dexamethasone and piperacillin/tazobactam. Given the atypical imaging features and concern for possible hematologic malignancy, video-assisted thoracoscopic biopsy was planned to obtain adequate tissue.

vignette:
A 67-year-old woman with a 4-day history of fever and cough was admitted to a local hospital, where SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed by nasopharyngeal PCR. Five days after admission, her respiratory status worsened, prompting intubation and transfer to the ICU. Her comorbidities included diabetes mellitus with dialysis-dependent nephropathy, angina, prior gastric cancer resection, and spinal‐canal stenosis; she was on an antiplatelet agent.  
On arrival: temperature 34 °C; blood pressure 110/65 mmHg; heart rate 102 beats/min; GCS E1VtM1 under deep sedation. Arterial blood gas (on pressure‐control ventilation: PEEP 8 cmH₂O, PiP 25 cmH₂O, FiO₂ 0.5) showed pH 7.309, PaCO₂ 41.5 mmHg, PaO₂ 78.2 mmHg.

vignette:
A 27-year-old woman who works as an agricultural laborer was referred with fatigue, malaise, anorexia, and epistaxis. On examination, she was pale, with eczematous plaques on her chest and proximal right arm, and had splenomegaly 6 cm below the costal margin. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 7.3 g/dL, white-cell count 4.0×10^9/L, and platelets 23×10^9/L. A peripheral-blood smear revealed lymphoblasts. Flow cytometry was positive for TdT, CD34, CD19, CD10, CD22, and HLA-DR, and bone marrow evaluation confirmed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The eczematous plaques were treated as contact dermatitis with topical methylprednisolone, resolving rapidly, and induction chemotherapy with hyper-CVAD was initiated. 

On day 8, she developed febrile neutropenia and received piperacillin–tazobactam. Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus species grew in blood cultures, prompting addition of teicoplanin. Persistent fever led to repeat cultures, which grew Enterococcus species, and teicoplanin was replaced with daptomycin. High-resolution chest CT showed nonspecific nodules under 1 cm, and serum galactomannan antigen was negative. After 10 days of fever with an absolute neutrophil count of 20/μL, she reported severe pain in her right arm radiating to her shoulder, suggesting herpes zoster; however, no vesicles were present. On examination, there was a very tender point in the upper lateral scapular region with an underlying vague mass. MRI of the right shoulder demonstrated a focal cystic necrotic lesion between the teres minor and teres major muscles.

A 28-year-old Hispanic man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis presented with a 10-day history of a pruritic eruption that began on the trunk and gradually spread to all extremities. Laboratory testing showed total bilirubin 28.9 mg/dL (reference <1.2), direct bilirubin 17.7 mg/dL (<0.3), AST 78 IU/L, ALT 42 IU/L, and alkaline phosphatase 231 IU/L. Gram, periodic acid–Schiff, and iron stains were negative. Punch biopsies of the chest and thigh were consistent with pityriasis rosea.

vignette:
A female infant was born at 35 weeks 4 days’ gestation, weighing 2152 g. She was one of monochorionic diamniotic twins; her identical twin died in utero at 24 weeks. Fetal ultrasound had shown microcephaly and ventricular enlargement. Postnatal MRI of the head revealed microcephaly, marked enlargement of both lateral ventricles without signs of elevated intracranial pressure, and severe thinning of the frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes; the temporal lobes, basal ganglia, thalamus, brain stem, and cerebellum were preserved. No intracranial hematoma or neoplastic lesions were seen. Family history was noncontributory. 

At 1 week of age, examination of the eyes showed very weak light reflexes bilaterally. The anterior chambers were slightly shallow, but there were no pupillary abnormalities, cataracts, strabismus, nystagmus, or ptosis. Funduscopic examination revealed mild optic nerve pallor with suspected peripapillary double-ring sign. The fundus had a faint reddish tone; retinal vessels appeared normal in caliber and reached the periphery. No chorioretinal dysplasia was noted.
